segments.text: Each token starts with a row of numbers called an embedding.
As an AI processes a message,
its layers update these numbers to reflect the surrounding context.
But when those new numbers are generated,
they might not exactly match the starting embedding of any existing token.
So how do they still represent meaning?
An exact match isn't actually necessary.
It's the relationships between the numbers that matter.
This map pictures those mathematical relationships as physical positions.
Let's build our space with three cities.
First, we add Dallas at exact coordinates of 32.78 north, 96.80 west.
Next, Mountain View at 37 north, 122 west.
Finally, we place New York City at 41 north, 74 west.
By defining just two numbers, latitude and longitude,
we lock in a known established identity within our map space.
This map introduces a new unknown position at 38 degrees north, 120 degrees west.
Look closely at the board.
Which of our three established cities is closest?
Mountain View is the closest.
Even without perfectly identical coordinates,
the short physical distance proves the match.
Next, we plot a second unknown position at 40 degrees north, 76 degrees west.
Which city is closest this time?
New York City is closest to the second point.
The coordinates didn't match perfectly in either case,
but measuring the distance allowed us to reliably find the closest match.
We can apply that exact same logic to more than two numbers.
Imagine evaluating drinks on a seven-point profile.
Sweetness, fizz, caffeine, and so on.
We use a vector of seven numbers to plot a drink's position in an abstract space.
This diagram outlines our abstract space.
Koch's seven coordinates plot it here.
Pepsi's scores are very similar to Koch's,
so it sits next to it in the soft drinks neighborhood.
Hot coffee scores are vastly different,
so it sits far away in the coffee and tea neighborhood.
We can't visually draw all seven dimensions,
but this simplified proximity map effectively clusters items
based on their closest multidimensional similarity.
Let's introduce Mystery Drink A.
Its first six numbers match the soft drinks.
To find the exact match, compare the final number, Citrus.
Mystery Drink A is 9, Koch is 1, Pepsi is 10.
Pepsi is closest because the gap is only 1.
Now look at Mystery Drink B.
Take a moment to compare its array of numbers with hot coffee's vector.
Hot coffee is the closest match,
because the ratings track closely across all seven dimensions.
AI relies on this exact principle scaled up.
Its embeddings have thousands of dimensions learned during training.
After the layers update a token,
AI calculates the smallest gaps across all those dimensions to find the closest match.
The physical position represents meaning
without requiring a mathematically perfect coordinate match.
Let's see how context physically moves a word in vector space.
Take the sentence,
the tiled cat sat on the mat during the May rainstorm.
It soon fell asleep.
On its own, the word it is completely ambiguous.
This 3D map shows the starting position of it,
with its initial coordinate numbers beginning
As the network processes the sentence,
the layers update the numbers for it to reflect its specific connection to cat.
The coordinates shift to 0.41, 0.06.
It remains a separate token,
but its new physical location mathematically maps its semantic connection
to the cat in this specific sentence.
Meaning is a position in vector space.
Similar meanings usually sit close together.
